## Q1-(a)

```{r}
read_and_merge <- function(){
  aux <- read_xpt("AUX_I.xpt")
  demo <- read_xpt("DEMO_I.xpt")
  merged <- inner_join(aux, demo, by = "SEQN")
  return(merged)
}

df_raw <- read_and_merge()
cat("Merged dataset dimensions (rows, columns):\n")
print(dim(df_raw))
```

I perform an inner join on the identifier `SEQN`. Only records that appear in both datasets are kept.We can now see the merged dimensions (4852,119)

## Q1-(b)

```{r}
clean_data <- function(df_raw){
  df_clean <- df_raw %>%
    mutate(
      # Gender: 1=Male, 2=Female
      gender = ifelse(RIAGENDR %in% c(99,999,-9,NA), NA, RIAGENDR),
      gender = factor(gender, levels = c(1,2), labels = c("Male","Female")),
      # Citizenship status
      citizenship = ifelse(DMDCITZN %in% c(99,999,-9,NA), NA, DMDCITZN),
      citizenship = factor(citizenship),
      # Income-to-poverty ratio (continuous)
      income_poverty = ifelse(INDFMPIR %in% c(99,999,-9,NA), NA, INDFMPIR),
      income_poverty = as.numeric(income_poverty),
      # Right ear tympanometric width
      tymp_right = ifelse(AUXTWIDR %in% c(99,999,-9,NA), NA, AUXTWIDR),
      tymp_right = as.numeric(tymp_right),
      # Left ear tympanometric width
      tymp_left = ifelse(AUXTWIDL %in% c(99,999,-9,NA), NA, AUXTWIDL),
      tymp_left = as.numeric(tymp_left)
    )
  return(df_clean)
}
df_clean <- clean_data(df_raw)
summary(df_clean %>% select(gender, citizenship, income_poverty, tymp_right, tymp_left))

```

I create a cleaned dataset starting from the merged data with 4582 observations.
All invalid/missing codes (-9, 99, 999) are recoded into R native `NA`.
`RIAGENDR` is converted to a labelled factor for gender.
`DMDCITZN` (citizenship status) is converted to a categorical factor.
`INDFMPIR` (income-to-poverty ratio) is kept as a continuous predictor.
`AUXTWIDR` and `AUXTWIDL` are the continuous tympanometric width outcomes for right and left ear, used in the Poisson regression models.

## Q1-(c)

```{r}
fit_poisson <- function(formula, data){
  mod <- glm(formula, family = poisson(link = "log"), data = data)
  irr_table <- tidy(mod, conf.int = TRUE, exponentiate = TRUE) %>%
    select(term, estimate, conf.low, conf.high, p.value) %>%
    rename(IRR = estimate, CI_low = conf.low, CI_high = conf.high, p_val = p.value)
  null_mod <- glm(update(formula, . ~ 1), family = poisson(link="log"), data = data)
  mcfadden_r2 <- 1 - as.numeric(logLik(mod)) / as.numeric(logLik(null_mod))
  fit_stats <- tibble(
    n = nrow(mod$model),
    AIC = AIC(mod),
    McFadden_pseudoR2 = mcfadden_r2
  )
  return(list(irr = irr_table, stats = fit_stats, model_obj = mod))
}
m1R <- fit_poisson(tymp_right ~ gender, df_clean)
m2R <- fit_poisson(tymp_right ~ gender + citizenship + income_poverty, df_clean)
m1L <- fit_poisson(tymp_left ~ gender, df_clean)
m2L <- fit_poisson(tymp_left ~ gender + citizenship + income_poverty, df_clean)
irr_all <- bind_rows(
  m1R$irr %>% mutate(Model = "1R: Right ~ Gender"),
  m2R$irr %>% mutate(Model = "2R: Right ~ Full"),
  m1L$irr %>% mutate(Model = "1L: Left ~ Gender"),
  m2L$irr %>% mutate(Model = "2L: Left ~ Full")
) %>%
  select(Model, term, IRR, CI_low, CI_high, p_val) %>%
  mutate(across(c(IRR, CI_low, CI_high), ~round(.x,3)), p_val = round(p_val,4))
stat_all <- bind_rows(
  m1R$stats %>% mutate(Model = "1R: Right ~ Gender"),
  m2R$stats %>% mutate(Model = "2R: Right ~ Full"),
  m1L$stats %>% mutate(Model = "1L: Left ~ Gender"),
  m2L$stats %>% mutate(Model = "2L: Left ~ Full")
) %>%
  select(Model, n, AIC, McFadden_pseudoR2) %>%
  mutate(across(c(AIC, McFadden_pseudoR2), ~round(.x,3)))
kable(irr_all, caption = "Incidence Risk Ratios from Poisson Regression Models", format = "html")
kable(stat_all, caption = "Model Fit Summary Statistics", format = "html")
```

Results are reported as incidence risk ratios (IRR). IRR \> 1 indicates a higher expected tympanometric width, and significance holds when the 95% CI does not contain 1.

In both simple and adjusted models, females have significantly greater tympanometric width than males. Citizenship category 2 is positively associated with wider width for both ears; citizenship category 7 is significant only for the right ear. Higher income-to-poverty ratio is linked to slightly smaller width.

The full adjusted models yield lower AIC and modest McFadden pseudo-\\(R\^2\\) (0.101 for right ear, 0.092 for left ear), showing citizenship and income improve model fit compared with gender-only models.

## Q1-(d)

This Poisson regression analysis examined associations between gender, citizenship, income-to-poverty ratio and tympanometric width. Females had significantly larger tympanometric width in both simple and fully adjusted models. Citizenship status and income-to-poverty ratio were also significant predictors. The full models had better fit than gender-only models. These findings suggest demographic and socioeconomic factors are associated with tympanometric width.

## Q2-(a)

```{r}
library(DBI)
library(RSQLite)
library(tidyverse)
library(microbenchmark)
con <- dbConnect(SQLite(), dbname = "sakila_master.db")
dbListTables(con)
## Method 1: SQL pull table first, then compute in R
pull_sql <- "SELECT store_id, active FROM customer;"
df_customer <- dbGetQuery(con, pull_sql)

q1_method1 <- function(){
  df_customer %>%
    mutate(active = as.integer(active)) %>% 
    group_by(store_id) %>%
    summarise(
      total_cust = n(),
      active_cust = sum(active),
      pct_active = active_cust / total_cust,
      .groups = "drop"
    )
}

## Method 2: single SQL
single_sql <- "
SELECT
  store_id,
  COUNT(*) AS total_cust,
  SUM(CAST(active AS INTEGER)) AS active_cust,
  ROUND(SUM(CAST(active AS INTEGER)) * 1.0 / COUNT(*), 4) AS pct_active
FROM customer
GROUP BY store_id;
"

q1_method2 <- function(){
  dbGetQuery(con, single_sql)
}

# benchmark
bm1 <- microbenchmark(
  R_after_sql = q1_method1(),
  single_sql = q1_method2(),
  times = 20
)

bm1
autoplot(bm1)

# print results
q1_method1()
q1_method2()

```

We calculated the total number of customers per store and the percentage of active customers for each store using two approaches.

Method 1: Extract the raw `customer` table with SQL and perform aggregation in R.

Method 2: Compute the final result directly with a single SQL query.Both methods return identical outputs:
Store 1 has 326 customers, with 97.55% active customers.
Store 2 has 273 customers, with 97.44% active customers.

From `microbenchmark`, the single-SQL method is substantially faster. The median runtime for the single SQL query is 460.29 microseconds, while the two-step approach (SQL pull + R manipulation) has a median runtime of 3108.09 microseconds. This is expected because the database engine optimizes aggregation natively, and the two-step method incurs extra overhead from transferring the full table to R and additional tidyverse operations.

## Q2-(b)

```{r}
## Method 1: SQL to pull all needed tables, then join in R
pull_sql <- "
SELECT s.first_name, s.last_name, a.city_id, c.country
FROM staff s
JOIN address a ON s.address_id = a.address_id
JOIN city ci ON a.city_id = ci.city_id
JOIN country c ON ci.country_id = c.country_id;
"
df_staff <- dbGetQuery(con, pull_sql)

q2_method1 <- function(){
  df_staff %>%
    select(first_name, last_name, country)
}

## Method 2: Single SQL query
single_sql <- "
SELECT s.first_name, s.last_name, c.country
FROM staff s
JOIN address a ON s.address_id = a.address_id
JOIN city ci ON a.city_id = ci.city_id
JOIN country c ON ci.country_id = c.country_id;
"
q2_method2 <- function(){
  dbGetQuery(con, single_sql)
}
# benchmark
bm2 <- microbenchmark(
  R_after_sql = q2_method1(),
  single_sql = q2_method2(),
  times = 20
)

bm2
autoplot(bm2)
# print results
q2_method1()
q2_method2()

```

Two methods produce identical results, listing staff names and their countries: Mike Hillyer is from Canada, and Jon Stephens is from Australia. The single SQL query runs faster. Its median runtime is 571.62 microseconds, compared with 1605.52 microseconds for the approach that pulls extra columns into R and selects variables afterwards. Joining tables and selecting required fields inside SQLite reduces data transfer overhead.

## Q2-(c)

```{r}
## Method1: Query raw data from SQL, then aggregate in R
pull_sql <- "
SELECT f.title, p.amount
FROM payment p
JOIN rental r ON p.rental_id = r.rental_id
JOIN inventory i ON r.inventory_id = i.inventory_id
JOIN film f ON i.film_id = f.film_id;
"
df_revenue <- dbGetQuery(con, pull_sql)

q3_method1 <- function(){
  df_revenue %>%
    group_by(title) %>%
    summarise(total_revenue = sum(amount, na.rm = TRUE)) %>%
    arrange(desc(total_revenue)) %>%
    slice(1)
}

## Method2: Single SQL query to compute and find the top film
single_sql <- "
SELECT f.title, SUM(p.amount) AS total_revenue
FROM payment p
JOIN rental r ON p.rental_id = r.rental_id
JOIN inventory i ON r.inventory_id = i.inventory_id
JOIN film f ON i.film_id = f.film_id
GROUP BY f.title
ORDER BY total_revenue DESC
LIMIT 1;
"

q3_method2 <- function(){
  dbGetQuery(con, single_sql)
}

# benchmark
bm3 <- microbenchmark(
  R_after_sql = q3_method1(),
  single_sql = q3_method2(),
  times = 20
)

bm3
autoplot(bm3)

# output result
q3_method1()
q3_method2()

```

Both methods identify **TELEGRAPH VOYAGE** as the film with the highest rental revenue, which totals \$231.73. Contrary to the previous two cases, the two‑step approach (fetch raw data to R and aggregate locally) runs faster here. Its mean runtime is 8.36 ms, while the single SQL query averages 46.21 ms. This may be caused by SQLite’s overhead for grouping and sorting on a large payment table.

## Q3-(a)

```{r}
library(tidyverse)

df <- read_csv("au-500.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)

q1 <- df %>%
  filter(!is.na(web) & web != "") %>%
  mutate(
    tld = str_extract(web, "\\.[^.]+$"),
    is_com = (tld == ".com")
  ) %>%
  summarise(
    total_valid = n(),
    com_count = sum(is_com),
    pct_com = mean(is_com) * 100
  )

q1
cat(sprintf("Percentage of websites that are .com: %.2f %% \n", q1$pct_com))

```

All website entries in this dataset are Australian domains such as `.com.au`, none end with the simple top-level domain `.com`. Hence the percentage of `.com` websites is 0.00%.

## Q3-(b)

```{r}
library(tidyverse)

q2 <- df %>%
  filter(!is.na(email) & email != "") %>%
  mutate(
    domain = str_extract(email, "(?<=@).+")
  ) %>%
  count(domain, sort = TRUE)

q2

```

We extracted the substring after `@` from each valid email to get the domain name, counted frequencies, and sorted in descending order. `hotmail.com` is the most frequent email domain in this dataset.

## Q3-(c)

```{r}
library(tidyverse)
q3 <- df %>%
  filter(!is.na(company_name) & company_name != "") %>%
  mutate(
   
    has_special_a = str_detect(company_name, "[^A-Za-z, ]"),
    
    has_special_b = str_detect(company_name, "[^A-Za-z, & ]")
  ) %>%
  summarise(
    total_valid = n(),
    prop_special_a = mean(has_special_a),
    prop_special_b = mean(has_special_b)
  )

q3

cat(sprintf(
  "Proportion with special characters (exclude comma, space): %.4f\nProportion with special characters (exclude comma, space, &): %.4f\n",
  q3$prop_special_a, q3$prop_special_b
))

```

Part (a): 9% of company names contain characters other than letters, commas and spaces. Part (b): when `&` is also treated as an allowed character, only 0.8% of company names have remaining special characters.

## Q3-(d)

```{r}
library(tidyverse)

reformat_phone <- function(x) {
  digits <- str_remove_all(x, "[^0-9]")
  if (nchar(digits) == 10) {
    str_c(str_sub(digits,1,4), " ", str_sub(digits,5,7), " ", str_sub(digits,8,10))
  } else {
    x
  }
}

q4 <- df %>%
  mutate(
    phone1_formatted = map_chr(phone1, reformat_phone),
    phone2_formatted = map_chr(phone2, reformat_phone)
  ) %>%
  select(phone1, phone1_formatted, phone2, phone2_formatted)

head(q4,10)

```

> We remove all non‑numeric symbols from raw phone numbers. Numbers with exactly 10 digits are rearranged into the `dddd ddd ddd` format; the original values are kept otherwise. The first ten records are displayed for verification.

## Q3-(e)

```{r}
library(tidyverse)

df <- df %>%
  mutate(
    unit_str = str_extract(address, regex("(Unit|Flat|Apt|Suite)\\s*(\\d+)", ignore_case = TRUE)),
    unit_num = str_extract(unit_str, "\\d+") %>% as.numeric()
  )

ggplot(df %>% filter(!is.na(unit_num)), aes(x = unit_num)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 15, fill = "steelblue", alpha = 0.7) +
  scale_x_log10() +
  labs(
    title = "Distribution of extracted unit numbers (log10 scale)",
    x = "Unit number (log10)",
    y = "Count"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
df %>% select(address, unit_str, unit_num) %>% head(10)

```

> The regex only captures unit numbers marked by keywords like Unit/Flat/Apt/Suite. Most addresses in this dataset do not follow this format, so nearly all extracted values are NA, resulting in an empty histogram.

## Q3-(f)

```{r}
library(tidyverse)
df <- df %>%
  mutate(
    hash_unit = str_extract(address, "#\\s*(\\d+)"),
    hash_unit_num = str_extract(hash_unit, "\\d+") %>% as.numeric(),
    all_unit_num = coalesce(unit_num, hash_unit_num)
  )

ggplot(df %>% filter(!is.na(all_unit_num)), aes(x = all_unit_num)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 15, fill = "coral", alpha = 0.7) +
  scale_x_log10() +
  labs(
    title = "Unit numbers extracted from # and Unit/Flat tags (log10)",
    x = "Unit number (log10)",
    y = "Count"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
df %>% select(address, unit_str, hash_unit, all_unit_num) %>% head(10)

```

We extract unit numbers from two patterns: `#number` and labels like Unit/Flat. `coalesce` combines the two sources. The histogram on a log10 scale shows the distribution of successfully extracted unit numbers.
